# Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking: A Comprehensive Study of Life, Art, and Advocacy
## Executive Summary
Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking (born 1950\) stands as a seminal figure in the landscape of contemporary Canadian realism. For more than five decades, Laking has dedicated her professional life to the documentation and interpretation of the Nova Scotian environment, establishing herself as a preeminent chronicler of the Bay of Fundy’s distinct geography and cultural vernacular . Operating primarily from her studio and gallery in Portapique, Colchester County, Laking has cultivated a formidable reputation for her technical mastery across multiple mediums—most notably watercolor, oil, and acrylic—while simultaneously expanding the boundaries of her creative practice into literature and theatre .

Laking's career is characterized by a dual commitment to aesthetic excellence and community advocacy. As a founding member of the Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia (PLANS), she has been instrumental in revitalizing the status of realist art within the Atlantic Canadian critical discourse . Her artistic contributions have been recognized with high honours, including the Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal and the Halifax Progress Club Woman of Excellence Award . Beyond the visual arts, Laking has demonstrated a profound engagement with social issues, authoring the play *Invisible Prisons* to address the pervasive reality of domestic violence .

This report provides an exhaustive biographical and critical analysis of Joy Laking’s career. It synthesizes data regarding her early influences, her idiosyncratic technical approaches to watercolor, her extensive exhibition history, her literary output, and her enduring impact on the cultural fabric of Nova Scotia.

## ---

**1\. Biography and Formative Years**

### 1.1 Origins and Familial Influence
Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking was born in 1950 in Owen Sound, Ontario . Her entry into the world of creative expression was arguably predetermined by a rich familial environment that valued artistic endeavor. She was born into a household where art was not merely a pastime but a vocation; her mother was a professional painter, and her father was a skilled craftsman known for creating intricate marionettes and toy trains . This early exposure to the rigors and rewards of creative production laid the foundation for Laking's future career.

The influence of her mother was particularly catalytic, serving as both a pedagogical model and a source of existential motivation. Laking painted alongside her mother from a young age, absorbing lessons in observation and technique that would later define her own pedagogy . However, it was a tragedy that solidified Laking's professional resolve. Her mother passed away prematurely in her early fifties from breast cancer, a loss that occurred roughly around the time Laking was completing her university studies .

In a revealing essay, Laking articulated the profound impact of this loss on her career trajectory. She noted that her mother’s death served as "an incentive to me to take the risk and practice my art with passion and commitment" . Confronted with the fragility of life, Laking decided "not to put it off," rejecting the safer, more conventional career paths often recommended to fine arts graduates in favor of immediate immersion in professional practice. This decision to bypass deferral and embrace the uncertainty of an artistic life was a direct response to her mother's unfulfilled potential, as her mother "never knew that I became an artist too" .

### 1.2 Education and Academic Background
Laking pursued formal academic training at the University of Guelph, where she majored in Fine Art, graduating in 1972 . Her time at Guelph provided her with a theoretical and practical foundation in the visual arts, yet Laking maintains a distinction regarding her technical expertise. Despite her degree, she identifies as largely self-taught in the medium of watercolor . This autodidactic approach to her primary medium allowed her to develop unconventional methods that diverge from academic norms, a topic explored in depth in the *Artistic Style* section of this report.

### 1.3 Migration to Nova Scotia and Geographic Adaptation
Following her graduation in 1972, Laking relocated to Nova Scotia, a move that would define the geographic and thematic scope of her life's work . She settled in the rural community of Bass River and later established her permanent base in Portapique .

This migration required a significant aesthetic adaptation. Laking was raised in the rugged, rock-strewn topography of Georgian Bay, Ontario—a landscape defined by open water and granite. In contrast, her new home on the shores of the Bay of Fundy presented a landscape of mudflats, salt marshes, and dramatic tidal shifts. Laking candidly admitted that she initially found the Nova Scotian terrain "very flat, no rocks... pastoral," and it did not immediately appeal to her sensibilities . However, the landscape "gradually grew on her" as she began to paint it . Over the ensuing forty-plus years, Laking has transformed this initial ambivalence into a profound intimacy, becoming one of the region's most dedicated visual interpreters .

### 1.4 Personal Life
Laking’s personal life is deeply intertwined with her artistic practice. She is married to Jim, who is frequently mentioned in the context of her travels and gallery operations . Together they have navigated the challenges of a professional artistic career, including the physical construction of her gallery. Laking is also a mother to three children 13, including a daughter, Danica . Her family often features in the periphery of her work, from the logistics of travel to the subject matter of her photography.

**2\. Artistic Style, Mediums, and Philosophy**

Laking’s artistic identity is multifaceted, spanning diverse mediums and grounded in a rigorous philosophical approach to observation. While she is best known as a watercolorist, her output includes oil painting, acrylics, printmaking, and fiber arts.

### 2.1 The Philosophy of "Seeing" vs. "Looking"
A central tenet of Laking’s artistic philosophy is the distinction between the passive act of "looking" and the active, cognitive discipline of "seeing." This distinction is not merely semantic but forms the core of her instructional and operational methodology. In an essay dedicated to her work, it was noted that Laking "observes the world around her with attentiveness, passion and keen interest," and that this "ability to see distinguishes her as an exceptional artist" .

Laking advocates for a process she describes as "noticing what you see." This involves stripping away intellectual preconceptions—the idea of what a "tree" or "ocean" looks like—and instead engaging with the raw visual data of light, shadow, and color relationship . When instructing others, she urges them to "just notice what you see and then draw it," emphasizing that in a "rushed world," the capacity to register visual impressions is a cultivated skill .

Her subject matter is characterized by "representational realism," yet it is democratic in its scope. Laking finds aesthetic value in conventional beauty as well as the mundane or industrial, stating that she sees "beauty in shapes and colours and contrasts whether it be traditional beauty or the back of a garbage truck" . This willingness to elevate the ordinary through careful observation is a hallmark of her realist approach.

### 2.2 Technical Mastery in Watercolor
Laking’s reputation was built on her watercolor landscapes, and her technique is noted for its divergence from traditional methods. Standard watercolor pedagogy typically dictates working from light to dark to preserve the luminosity of the paper for highlights. Laking, however, employs a method that works the "opposite from the usual approach," often laying in dark pigments first .

She describes this idiosyncratic process as "kind of magic," noting that "you put a hint of colour here and there and suddenly the paper turns into a flower" . By establishing her darks early, Laking achieves a depth and contrast that gives her watercolors a structural solidity often lacking in the medium. This technique allows for "spontaneity and lightness," particularly in her plein air work, where speed and decisiveness are required .

### 2.3 The Plein Air Discipline
Laking is a devoted practitioner of *en plein air* painting, a method that requires the artist to work outdoors, directly in front of the subject, regardless of environmental conditions. Her stamina and commitment to this practice are well-documented. She is known to hike with a backpack and stool to remote locations, remaining in the same spot for up to six hours to capture the shifting light and tides .

This direct engagement with nature allows her to capture the specific atmospheric conditions of the Bay of Fundy. She has spent years painting the tides, a subject that demands rapid execution and keen observation of changing water levels . Her plein air work is characterized by an "engaging spontaneity," capturing the immediate energy of the landscape .

### 2.4 Studio Practice and "Winter Works"
Laking’s practice is seasonally bifurcated. While the warmer months are dedicated to plein air painting, the winter months necessitate a retreat to the studio. This shift in environment precipitates a shift in process.

* **Methodology:** In the studio, Laking utilizes sketches and photographs taken from various angles to compose larger, more complex works. She engages in a process of "rearranging them and looking to see if a composition for a painting might emerge" . 
* **Timeframe:** Unlike the immediate execution of plein air work, studio paintings may take days, weeks, or even months to resolve. 
* **Stylistic Shift:** Studio works often become "more generalized, less realistic" as the scale increases, allowing Laking to explore composition and abstraction more freely than in her location work .

### 2.5 Diversification of Mediums: The 2007 "Explosion"
While watercolor defined her early career, Laking has consistently expanded her technical repertoire. In 2007, following her recovery from a serious health issue and inspired by extensive travel and a new marriage, she experienced what she described as an "explosion of creativity" . This period marked a significant broadening of her artistic output:

* **Oils and Acrylics:** She began working increasingly in oils and acrylics, enjoying the "slippery delicious medium" of oil sticks and the ability to "push and shove" the painting into being . 
* **Printmaking:** The gallery features her handmade serigraphs, demonstrating her skill in print media . 
* **Fiber Arts:** Laking engages in dying wool, hooking, and felting. She hooked her first rug, *Full and Starry Night over Five Islands*, during a two-month road trip to Alaska . 
* **Photography:** Laking has also exhibited photography, notably in the 2007 exhibition *Here and Away — Seeing with Passionate Eyes*. Her photography is noted for focusing on people and movement, a subject matter often absent from her landscape paintings .

**3\. The Joy Laking Gallery: A Model of Independence**

### 3.1 Establishment and Infrastructure
In the late 1980s, Laking and her husband took the significant step of establishing the **Joy Laking Gallery** at their home in Portapique, Nova Scotia . Located at 6730 Highway 2, the gallery is a physical manifestation of Laking’s commitment to living and working in rural Nova Scotia . The gallery was purpose-built to display her work, allowing her to bypass the constraints of the traditional gallery system and connect directly with her audience.

### 3.2 Operations and Commercial Activity
The gallery operates seasonally and by appointment, reflecting the rhythms of Laking’s painting schedule.

* **Summer Operations:** It is typically open daily from late June until early September . 
* **Off-Season:** The gallery remains accessible "by chance or by appointment" throughout the rest of the year . 
* **Inventory:** The space features a comprehensive collection of her output, including original paintings, serigraphs, prints, greeting cards, and her published books .

The gallery also functions as a community hub, hosting events such as book launches where Laking serves tea and signs copies of her works, fostering a personal connection with her collectors .

**4\. Exhibition History and Professional Milestones**

Laking’s career trajectory is marked by a steady ascent from regional solo shows to major national exhibitions. Her exhibition history reflects both her individual development and her role in the broader realist movement.

### 4.1 Chronology of Solo Exhibitions
Laking’s solo career began gaining momentum in the early 1980s.

| Year | Exhibition Title / Venue | Location | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1982** | *Flowers of Nova Scotia* at **Mount Saint Vincent University Art Gallery** | Halifax, NS | First major solo exhibition; established national reputation |
| **1983** | **Gallery 1889** | Tatamagouche, NS | 7 |
| **1984** | **Royal Botanical Gardens** | Burlington, ON | Display of 50 watercolors; significant national exposure |
| **1985** | **Owens Art Gallery**, Mount Allison University | Sackville, NB | First New Brunswick solo exhibition |
| **1987** | **Gallery 1889** | Tatamagouche, NS | 7 |
| **1989** | *Joy Laking: Winter Work* at **Art Gallery of Nova Scotia (AGNS)** | Halifax, NS | Career-defining exhibition; subsequently toured regionally for a year (1989-1990) |
| **1990** | **Royal Botanical Gardens** | Burlington, ON | 7 |
| **1996** | **Division Street Church** | Owen Sound, ON | Exhibition in her hometown |
| **2007** | *Here and Away — Seeing with Passionate Eyes* | Truro, NS | Photography exhibition with Laurie Gunn |

### 4.2 Group Exhibitions and Collaborative Projects
Laking has been a key figure in collaborative efforts to promote Nova Scotian art.

* Capture 2014: Nova Scotia Realism (2014): 
 Laking was a driving force behind this pivotal exhibition at the Dalhousie University Art Gallery. Curated by Tom Smart, the exhibition sought to validate and celebrate the realist tradition in Nova Scotia. Laking exhibited alongside notable peers such as Tom Forrestall, Steven Rhude, Shelley Mitchell, Paul Hannon, Susan Paterson, Ed Huner, and Gord MacDonald . The exhibition opened in January 2014 and ran until March . 
* PLANS Touring Exhibitions (2014): 
 Following the Capture 2014 show, the PLANS group continued to exhibit collectively. In April 2014, they exhibited at the Nova Scotia Archives, followed by shows in Truro and Inverness in September and October of that year . 
* Painting in Situ (2015): 
 Laking participated in the "Painting in Situ" event in Parrsboro, NS. This plein air painting event and subsequent exhibition featured Laking alongside artists Susan Paterson, Susan Tooke, Richard Rudnicki, and Bill Rogers . 
* Elizabeth Bishop House Residency (2021): 
 In February 2021, Laking and fellow artist Susan Paterson spent a week in residence at the Elizabeth Bishop House in Great Village, NS. Due to extreme cold, they focused on painting the interior of the historic home, capturing the light through lace curtains and the "warmth, coziness and history" of the space .

**5\. Advocacy for Realism: PLANS**

A defining aspect of Laking’s later career is her activism on behalf of the realist style. Around 2009-2010, Laking became a founding member of **PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia)**.2

### 5.1 The Mission of PLANS
The formation of PLANS was a direct response to a perceived marginalization of realism within the established art world. Laking and her peers felt that realism was "discriminated against" by public galleries and curators who favored conceptual and abstract modalities . The group’s objective was to advocate for the validity, technical difficulty, and contemporary relevance of realist art.

### 5.2 Impact
The efforts of PLANS culminated in the *Capture 2014* exhibition, which brought institutional recognition to the movement. By organizing and exhibiting collectively, Laking and her colleagues succeeded in creating a platform for realism that might not have been achieved individually.

**6\. Literary Contributions and Illustration**

Laking’s creative output extends beyond the easel into the realm of publishing. She has had a significant career as both an illustrator and an author.

### 6.1 Early Illustration Work
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Laking illustrated children's books for the Nova Scotia Department of Lands and Forests. These works were often educational, dealing with environmental themes.

* ***The Brook and the Woodcutter*** (1979): Written by Gary Saunders and illustrated by Laking . This book is noted as an "early environmental warning," reflecting a conservationist ethos . 
* ***The Man Who Couldn't Stop Sneezing*** (1982): Also written by Gary Saunders and illustrated by Laking .

Despite enjoying the illustrative process, Laking found the financial compensation inadequate for a full-time career. Consequently, she pivoted towards self-publishing calendars of her paintings, which proved to be a more sustainable revenue stream and helped popularize her imagery .

### 6.2 Authored Publications
In recent years, Laking has published books that synthesize her visual art with her writing, offering a more holistic view of her creative vision.

#### *The Painted Province: Nova Scotia Through an Artist's Eyes*** **(2020)
Published by Pottersfield Press, this book is arguably Laking’s magnum opus in print.

* **Scope:** The book features over 200 paintings (oil, acrylic, and watercolor) depicting 40 different locations across Nova Scotia, from the southwestern shores of Meteghan to the highlands of Neil's Harbour . 
* **Design and Utility:** Laking designed the book with a specific utility in mind. It is tablet-sized (9.75 x 6.75 inches) to fit conveniently in a car’s glove compartment . Furthermore, she included GPS coordinates for the location of each painting, effectively turning the art book into a travel guide that encourages families to explore the province . 
* **Narrative Element:** The visual content is accompanied by "word pictures"—Laking’s poetic descriptions of the locations and her painting process . 
* **Reception:** Reviewers praised the book for its ability to evoke the specific "feeling" of rural Nova Scotia, with one reviewer noting that the images transported them back to their childhood .

#### *The Colours of Winter*** **(2019)
Also published by Pottersfield Press, this children's book focuses on the winter landscape . It reflects Laking’s long-standing fascination with winter light and snow, themes she explored in her *Winter Work* exhibition at the AGNS.

**7\. Social Advocacy and Theatre: *Invisible Prisons***

Perhaps the most striking divergence from her visual work is Laking’s contribution to social theatre. In response to the pervasive issue of domestic violence, Laking wrote the play ***Invisible Prisons***.

### 7.1 Origin and Content
*Invisible Prisons* is a collection of thirteen monologues based on true stories . Laking interviewed 14 women (and two men) to construct a narrative that exposes the complex mechanics of abuse. The play illustrates how "links of alienation, domination, isolation, and violation" are forged to create an "invisible prison" around the victim .

### 7.2 Production and Impact
* **Premiere:** The play was performed in Truro in March 2013, directed by Bryden MacDonald and produced by Lenore Zann, utilizing members of the Truro Theatre Society . 
* **Continued Relevance:** The play continued to be produced in 2014 . 
* **Educational Use:** In 2020, the play was performed virtually by the Zucker School of Medicine in New York, demonstrating its relevance beyond the local context . Laking has made the script available for free to community groups, schools, and police departments, viewing the work as a tool for education and social change rather than a commercial product .

**8\. Community Leadership and Board Service**

Laking has maintained a rigorous commitment to community service, serving on the boards of diverse cultural and social organizations. Her leadership roles reflect her dual interests in the arts and social welfare.

### 8.1 Institutional Boards
Laking has served on the governing bodies of the following organizations:

* **Art Gallery of Nova Scotia (AGNS):** Served two terms on the Board of Governors . 
* **Robert Pope Foundation:** Board member since 1997\. This foundation explores the intersection of art and medicine . 
* **The Elizabeth Bishop Society:** Board member . 
* **Ship's Company Theatre:** Board member . 
* **Ivar Mendez International Foundation:** Board member .

### 8.2 Social Welfare Organizations
* **Third Place Transition House:** Laking has served on the board of this organization, which supports women and children fleeing violence, aligning with the themes of her play *Invisible Prisons*.2

### 8.3 Community Events
Laking is a regular participant in the **Terry Fox Run** in Great Village, Nova Scotia. She has been noted as an active supporter of this cancer research fundraiser for many years, contributing to the community spirit of the event .

**9\. Awards and Honours**

Laking’s extensive contributions have been formally recognized by provincial and national bodies.

| Year | Award | Granting Body | Significance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **2006** | **Philatelic Selection** | Canada Post | Painting of a pink grapefruit selected for a stamp to raise funds for the Jewish General Hospital |
| **2009** | **Woman of Excellence Award** | Halifax Progress Club | Recognition of community and professional impact |
| **2012** | **Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal** | Government of Canada | Awarded for significant contributions to the arts and community |
| **2016** | **Artist Residency** | Port Bickerton | 6 |
| **2020/21** | **Lifetime Achievement Award** | Cobequid Arts Council | Honoring a sustained career of excellence |
| **N/A** | **Elected Member** | Society of Canadian Artists (SCA) | Professional peer recognition |

**10\. Collections**

Joy Laking’s work is held in major public and corporate collections, serving as a permanent record of her artistic vision.

* **Art Gallery of Nova Scotia (Permanent Collection):** Includes works such as *Brigitte's Window* (1984) . 
* **Nova Scotia Art Bank:** Includes works such as *Lily* (1984) and *Farewell to Summer* (1987) . 
* **International Reach:** Her work has been cited as being in collections in the UK and Europe, and she has painted in numerous countries globally .

**11\. Conclusion**

Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking’s career is a testament to the power of sustained observation and community engagement. From her early decision to pursue art in the wake of personal tragedy to her decades-long documentation of the Bay of Fundy, Laking has built a body of work that is both aesthetically rigorous and deeply rooted in place. Her innovations in watercolor technique, her advocacy for the realist tradition through PLANS, and her courageous exploration of social issues through *Invisible Prisons* mark her as a significant cultural figure in Atlantic Canada. Through her gallery, her books, and her teaching, she continues to invite the public not just to look at Nova Scotia, but to truly *see* it.

The 1984 exhibition at Royal Botanical Gardens displayed 50 of Laking's watercolors.
The 1984 exhibition at Royal Botanical Gardens provided Laking with significant national exposure.
Laking had her first New Brunswick solo exhibition at Owens Art Gallery, Mount Allison University in Sackville, NB in 1985.
Laking exhibited at Gallery 1889 in Tatamagouche, NS in 1987.
Laking had a career-defining exhibition, *Joy Laking: Winter Work*, at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia (AGNS) in Halifax, NS in 1989.
The *Joy Laking: Winter Work* exhibition subsequently toured regionally for a year (1989-1990).
Laking exhibited at Royal Botanical Gardens in Burlington, ON in 1990.
Laking had an exhibition in her hometown at Division Street Church in Owen Sound, ON in 1996.
Laking had a photography exhibition, *Here and Away - Seeing with Passionate Eyes*, with Laurie Gunn in Truro, NS in 2007.
Laking was a driving force behind the pivotal exhibition *Capture 2014: Nova Scotia Realism* at the Dalhousie University Art Gallery.
*Capture 2014: Nova Scotia Realism* was curated by Tom Smart.
The *Capture 2014: Nova Scotia Realism* exhibition sought to validate and celebrate the realist tradition in Nova Scotia.
Laking exhibited alongside notable peers such as Tom Forrestall, Steven Rhude, Shelley Mitchell, Paul Hannon, Susan Paterson, Ed Huner, and Gord MacDonald in *Capture 2014*.
The *Capture 2014* exhibition opened in January 2014 and ran until March.
Following the *Capture 2014* show, the PLANS group continued to exhibit collectively.
In April 2014, the PLANS group exhibited at the Nova Scotia Archives.
The PLANS group had shows in Truro and Inverness in September and October of 2014.
Laking participated in the "Painting in Situ" event in Parrsboro, NS in 2015.
The "Painting in Situ" event was a plein air painting event and subsequent exhibition.
The "Painting in Situ" event featured Laking alongside artists Susan Paterson, Susan Tooke, Richard Rudnicki, and Bill Rogers.
In February 2021, Laking and fellow artist Susan Paterson spent a week in residence at the Elizabeth Bishop House in Great Village, NS.
Due to extreme cold, Laking and Paterson focused on painting the interior of the historic Elizabeth Bishop House.
Laking and Paterson captured the light through lace curtains and the "warmth, coziness and history" of the Elizabeth Bishop House.
The formation of PLANS was a direct response to a perceived marginalization of realism within the established art world.
Laking and her peers felt that realism was "discriminated against" by public galleries and curators who favored conceptual and abstract modalities.
The objective of PLANS was to advocate for the validity, technical difficulty, and contemporary relevance of realist art.
The efforts of PLANS culminated in the *Capture 2014* exhibition.
The *Capture 2014* exhibition brought institutional recognition to the realist movement.
By organizing and exhibiting collectively, Laking and her colleagues succeeded in creating a platform for realism that might not have been achieved individually.
In the late 1970s and early 1980s, Laking illustrated children's books for the Nova Scotia Department of Lands and Forests.
These children's books were often educational, dealing with environmental themes.
*The Brook and the Woodcutter* (1979) was written by Gary Saunders and illustrated by Laking.
*The Brook and the Woodcutter* is noted as an "early environmental warning," reflecting a conservationist ethos.
*The Man Who Couldn't Stop Sneezing* (1982) was written by Gary Saunders and illustrated by Laking.
Despite enjoying the illustrative process, Laking found the financial compensation inadequate for a full-time career.
Laking pivoted towards self-publishing calendars of her paintings.
Self-publishing calendars proved to be a more sustainable revenue stream for Laking.
Self-publishing calendars helped popularize Laking's imagery.
In recent years, Laking has published books that synthesize her visual art with her writing.
Laking's books offer a more holistic view of her creative vision.
*Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* is published by Pottersfield Press.
*Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* is arguably Laking's magnum opus in print.
The book *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* features over 200 paintings (oil, acrylic, and watercolor).
The paintings in *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* depict 40 different locations across Nova Scotia, from the southwestern shores of Meteghan to the highlands of Neil's Harbour.
Laking designed the book *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* with a specific utility in mind.
*Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* is tablet-sized (9.75 x 6.75 inches) to fit conveniently in a car's glove compartment.
Laking included GPS coordinates for the location of each painting in *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing*.
*Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* effectively turns the art book into a travel guide that encourages families to explore the province.
The visual content in *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* is accompanied by "word pictures"—Laking's poetic descriptions of the locations and her painting process.
Reviewers praised *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* for its ability to evoke the specific "feeling" of rural Nova Scotia.
One reviewer noted that the images in *Joy Laking: The Art of Seeing* transported them back to their childhood.
*Winter's Light* is also published by Pottersfield Press.
*Winter's Light* is a children's book that focuses on the winter landscape.
*Winter's Light* reflects Laking's long-standing fascination with winter light and snow.
Laking explored themes of winter light and snow in her *Winter Work* exhibition at the AGNS.
*Invisible Prisons* is a collection of thirteen monologues based on true stories.
Laking interviewed 14 women (and two men) to construct a narrative for *Invisible Prisons* that exposes the complex mechanics of abuse.
The play *Invisible Prisons* illustrates how "links of alienation, domination, isolation, and violation" are forged to create an "invisible prison" around the victim.
The play *Invisible Prisons* was performed in Truro in March 2013.
*Invisible Prisons* was directed by Bryden MacDonald.
*Invisible Prisons* was produced by Lenore Zann, utilizing members of the Truro Theatre Society.
The play *Invisible Prisons* continued to be produced in 2014.
In 2020, the play *Invisible Prisons* was performed virtually by the Zucker School of Medicine in New York.
The virtual performance of *Invisible Prisons* by the Zucker School of Medicine demonstrates its relevance beyond the local context.
Laking has made the script of *Invisible Prisons* available for free to community groups, schools, and police departments.
Laking views *Invisible Prisons* as a tool for education and social change rather than a commercial product.
Laking has served two terms on the Board of Governors for the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia (AGNS).
Laking has been a board member of the Robert Pope Foundation since 1997.
The Robert Pope Foundation explores the intersection of art and medicine.
Laking is a board member of The Elizabeth Bishop Society.
Laking is a board member of Ship's Company Theatre.
Laking is a board member of the Ivar Mendez International Foundation.
Laking has served on the board of Third Place Transition House.
Third Place Transition House supports women and children fleeing violence.
Laking's service on the board of Third Place Transition House aligns with the themes of her play *Invisible Prisons*.
Laking is a regular participant in the Terry Fox Run in Great Village, Nova Scotia.
Laking has been noted as an active supporter of the Terry Fox Run cancer research fundraiser for many years.
Laking contributes to the community spirit of the Terry Fox Run event.

By Linda Harrington 

Although there was avery heavy mist as registra-tion for the Second Annual Great Village Terry Fox Run began, orgainzer Debbie Smith says it only dampened the paperwork not the spir-it of those who came to par-ticipate in the day’s events. Twenty-six people and four canines completed the almost 8 km route, either on foot or bicycle. The youngest, being 7 year old Connor Harrison, who walked a km for each year of his life and was proud to do so! Colby, Haley and Michael Spencer enjoyed riding the course on their bicycles. When the sun finally came out, the event turned into a real social event. Participants and others, who stopped by to make a con-tribution, enjoyed apples donated by the Masstown Market and corn grown and cooked by Farmer Keith! “It was great to see new faces, and of course the reg-ulars, who have supported our run in the past two years,” says Debbie Smith. After the pledges and donations were added up a grand total of $1630 was realized, almost $200 more than last year. Debbie would like to thank everyone for their support adding, “We are hoping for an even bet-ter turnout next year for the 35th anniversary of Terry’s dream.” The winner of the Terry Fox t-shirt was Charlotte Smith. 

By Linda Harrington 

The grand opening for “Across the Surface”, an art exhibit featuring the work of eight of Nova Scotia’s most prominent realist artists, was held at NSCC McCarthy Art Gallery in Truro on Sept. 5th. Local artist Joy Laking says the idea for the exhibit began 5 years ago when a group of artists were talking about why realism is so discriminat-ed against what they could do to change this. Eight organizers formed PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia), with a goal to raise the profile of realist painting in Nova Scotia. The group consists of Tom Forrestall, Ed Huner, Paul Hannon, Steven Rhude, Susan Paterson, Shelley Mitchell, Gordon MacDonald and Joy Laking. With a $30,000 grant from the Robert Pope Foundation, the group hired independent curator Tom Smart to put an exhibit together. The “Capture 2014” exhibit fea-tured one piece from 28 artists and has been touring several Universities in Nova Scotia. On the success of the first exhibit, PLANS decided to put together another exhibit featuring several paintings by each of the 8 founding artists and they called this “Across the Surface”. The exhibit opened at the Archives of Nova Scotia, then moved to Truro, and after Sept. 25th will move to Inverness Cultural Center during Celtic Colours. Joy Laking is excited to have the exhibit here in Truro, close to her home in Portaupique. “We have secured a grant so school children can come and visit the show, and I will give them a tour,” she says, her eyes sparkling with excite-ment. Joy Laking will host her annual Open House Exhibition at her studio, 6730 Hwy #2, in Portaupique on October 18, 19, 25 &26 from 10AM until 5PM. This year’s exhibit features Joy’s paint-ings and sketches done in India as well as many new oil paintings, acrylics and water-colours of Nova Scotia. The McCarthy Gallery, a partnership between the NSCC and Truro Arts Society, has hosted 200 art shows since its opening, averaging about 6 to 10 shows/year.

School is in session... DRIVE CAREFULLY 

By Dick Akerman 

A description of the 1889 fire in Great Village, taken directly from the day journal of Dr. J.L. Peppard, the village doctor: “Thursday, November 21, 1889 House burned. The fire originated in the store of J.M. Blaikie, Esquire, on the morn-ing of Nov.21st - at twenty minutes to four, am. Burned store, post office and barn of J.M. Blaikie–Brazilla Davidson’s house and stable, my house – Mrs. Fulton’s house–her barn was burned to stop the flames.–this has been the greatest destruction since this place was set-tled. The total loss supposed to be $20,000. After the fire I went to Truro, –to look after insurance on house – we moved into the Thomas E Spencer house.” A few months earlier, the journal describes the birth of his daughter, a few months after the fire he notes the death of that daughter, he attributed the death to the cold and subsequent menin-gitis she was afflicted with as aresult of the fire. He reports going to the court hearings of the young men who were involved with the fire, and on the back page of a later journal was the list of materials needed to build a replacement home. The circle on map # 302 of the “A. F. Church” map covers the burned area, as does the circle on the 1889 “ Currie” map, which is an artist’s rendition. 

Dick Akerman has been compiling information on behalf of the Colchester Historical Museum Archives, and is published monthly in the Shoreline Journal.

Church Maps” to pin point the circa 1875 location of a Colchester site of historical importance, and connect it to an archival photograph of that site, in that frame. This article, “Historic Sites” has been published in the “Shoreline” for over three years, and features period photographs of interesting sites along the Cobequid shore, homes, stores, hotels, mines, bridges, etc. The photographs are reinforced with amap location, taken from the famous “Church” map of Colchester County.

She is an elected member of the Society of Canadian Artists and received the 2009 Woman of Excellence Award and the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Medal.

The Gallery is open by chance or by **appointment. If you would like to book an appointment, please give us a call at****902-890-8730.**

Overview
--------

Located on a Bay of Fundy salt marsh, the Joy Laking Gallery, located on Hwy 2, between Great Village and Bass River, welcomes visitors to come and enjoy the gold finches, the gardens, the view of the bay and of courses Joy’s paintings.

For over fifty years, Joy has captured the beauty of Nova Scotia and the world in watercolour, oil and acrylic paintings. She has had national solo exhibitions including one at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia that subsequently toured for a year.

In addition to the paintings, the Gallery also offers greeting cards and prints. Located at 6730 Hwy 2, Portapique, the Gallery is well signed, and is open daily June 28 until September 4 from 11am until 4pm and other times of day and of the year by chance or by appointment.

The website [www.joylakinggallery.com](http://www.joylakinggallery.com/) features all of Joy’s recent work.

1 

> Essay on Joy Laking
> by Shawna Macivor
> from the book "Following the Vision" (six Nova Scotia Artists)
> Published by the Robert Pope Foundation and
> Distributed by Nimbus Press

The Art of Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking S.C.A. 

A couple of years ago, I had the chance to travel in Ireland with a high school friend from 

Owen Sound, Ontario, the artist Joy Joy Laking. We rambled along the west coast, with 

Joy sketching and taking photos. On e afternoon we were perched on a rock near the sea 

and Joy was absorbed in her watercolours. The shoreline, the distant hills and an 

exquisite violet -coloured, sky -reflecting sea appeared under her brush. Unnerved by my 

staring, she suddenly stopped and fi shed out of her bag a small 5”x7” square of stiff 

watercolour paper and a black Staedtler 0.5 pen. “Here,” she said, “try it. Just draw what 

you see. I mean,” she paused, “just notice what you see and then draw it.” 

That comment about noticing what you see struck me then, and now, as quintessential 

Joy. In our rushed world, we receive a myriad of impressions but most of us register very 

little. Joy Laking observes the world around her with attentiveness, passion and keen 

interest. Her ability to see disting uishes her as an exceptional artist as much as her 

obvious talent for drawing and composition and her mastery of the medium of 

watercolour. 

It is fitting that an essay on Joy Laking’s painting and approach to her work should be 

published by the Robert Pope Foundation. Joy has served on the Board of the Nova 

Scotia -based Robert Pope Foundation since 1997. This foundation, bridging art and 

medicine, was set up as a service organization and a memorial to a dedicated and gifted 

artist, Robert Pope, who died of cancer in his early thirties. 

Living life fully and dying with dignity were lessons Joy learned at home. “My Mother 

was an artist and a major influence on my life. She died young – in her early fifties, of 

breast cancer. She died just about the time whe n I was graduating from fine art at 

university and pondering my future. Her death was an incentive to me to take the risk and 

practice my art with passion and commitment. I decided not to put it off. She never knew 

that I became an artist too. I miss her every day.” 

The novelist, Virginia Woolf, ended her novel, The Waves , with the declaration, “ Against 

you I will fling myself, unvanquished and unyielding, O Death !” Art is linked with life 

and death in a fundamental way. The best artists appear to break th e bonds of time and 

space. E.M. Forster captured the glory and the immense labour of that creative effort, 

acclaiming Woolf’s novels as “ trophies won by the mind from the matter, its enemy and 

its friend .” 

Joy began striving for artistic ‘trophies’ at an early age. Making art was a family affair. 

On her mother’s side were generations of English jet carvers who carved the 2

metamorphosed coal into buttons, broaches, crosses and funeral ornaments in Victorian 

England. Not only did her mother paint, but her fat her built marionette puppets and 

trains, tinted photographs and eventually began painting too. Both parents won art 

competitions as children and both had their paintings featured in the window of 

Eaton’s in Hamilton, Ontario. As a child, Joy thought all ho uses had an ‘art drawer’ in 

most rooms and was surprised to find, later, that not all houses came so well -equipped. 

Her mother nurtured the creative process. She would set out materials and leave her three 

children to make their own way. As a child, Joy also accompanied her mother on frequent 

excursions to paint the Georgian Bay scenery. While she loved these trips, Joy was 

frustrated by the gulf between her own productions and her mother’s. “ I always felt 

terribly inadequate. I couldn’t produce what I sa w or what my mother could do. It didn’t 

please me.” 

For the emerging artist this was perhaps an ideal environment: stimulation, 

encouragement and the bar set high. But another, more surprising influence shaped her 

development as a visual artist: poor eyes ight. One day, in grade two, Joy carefully copied 

from the blackboard a set of math questions. She answered them perfectly. The only 

problem was that the questions in her notebook were not the questions written on the 

blackboard. Her teacher recommended ge tting her eyes tested. 

With new glasses on her nose, Joy gazed, enthralled, at a ravishing, unguessed -at, world. 

“I had always thought grass was a flat green. I was shocked to see individual blades of 

grass. Suddenly the world was revealed in astonishing focus and form, and I could see all 

the subtle colour changes. I wanted to look and look at the multi -hued richness of 

everything.” 

Perhaps this sudden awakening to the close -up world was the initial spur to a 

preoccupation informing her adult work: met iculous rendering of abundant detail. Every 

paint flake, stone fissure, seashell barnacle and flower petal is caught precisely. 

It was easy for Joy, as a child, to lose herself in make -believe. She was born with a 

powerful imagination. The line between h er daily world and the created world was very 

thin. “ Sometimes my parents dressed the marionette puppets they made in clothes made 

from the same material as my own clothes. I recall a red plaid in particular. I regarded 

these puppets as my own relations. ”

As it turned out, the artist’s keen imagination and intense absorption in her art helped 

ensure her survival through a difficult marriage. 

In June 1999, when she was almost fifty, Joy leapt with a backpack from a wave -rocked 

boat on to Quirpon Island, just off Newfoundland. She spent almost two weeks there, 

totally alone except for her paints and her journal. It was a pivotal time. In the silence and 

the daily conquering of fear – it was frigid, stormy, and the island was uninhabited – Joy 

was brought f ace to face with her own circumstances. 3

“The year before I left the marriage, I had 12 days on that island all alone. It snowed 

every day, and all I had was one book. I painted with freezing fingers through all the 

daylight hours, and I realized that I c ould survive alone.” 

She had married and moved from Ontario to Nova Scotia after graduating from the 

University of Guelph in 1972 with a degree in fine art. She and her husband settled in 

Bass River on the shore of the Bay of Fundy in Colchester County. Between the years 

1980 and 1985 they had three children: Kelsey, Danica and Yolande. 

From the beginning, Joy chose to work with watercolor, in a realistic style. It was not a 

trendy choice in the 1970s, nor was it what she had studied at university where the focus 

was on acrylics and abstract art. But she wanted a healthy environment without the 

solvents and other chemicals associated with oils. And it was the physical world that 

inspired her to paint. 

She did not warm to the Maritime scenery immediatel y. Growing up in Grey County, 

Ontario, Joy had lovingly absorbed the landscape of limestone rock, grey waves, rolling 

hills, pines and maples, and cedar swamps. “ I lived that scenery. Perhaps you do 

internalize your first scenery no matter what it is, bu t the Georgian Bay landscape was 

deeply imprinted on me and I was in tune with and deeply inspired by the work of the 

Group of Seven .” 

One day, searching for something to paint in her new province, she took her materials 

down to Peggy’s Cove to sketch a group of fishing men near their boats. She became 

engrossed in the scene, staying the whole day, watching and sketching men doing their 

routine chores and chatting. Missing friends and family from Ontario, she thought these 

people seemed ‘very friendly’. 

“They were people as friendly shapes. I saw them as faceless, but really nice appealing 

shapes. I played with the shapes to make a pleasing composition and then I learned how 

to handle watercolour by just moving the paint around inside the shapes. I sp ent a year 

and a half doing an entire series - I called them the 'potato people'. They helped me feel 

less lonely.” 

But the artist’s inner landscape surfaced even in the midst of painting these friendly 

beings. “One of the paintings I did at that time wa s one of me in prison garb playing 

solitaire in a striped uniform with a number on it, and the number was the date of my 

mother’s death .” 

Isolated in the country, and seeing very few people in those early days, Joy was 

vulnerable to the view that as an ar tist she was not really contributing; she might be just 

playing, with possibly nothing to show in the end. But sustained by a core belief in the 

value of her art that went deeper than these fears, she carried on. Caring for her children 

also helped to giv e her a sense of purpose and increased her compassion and awareness. 4

“I loved mothering – and even home -schooled them all for a year. The children were 

important to my survival. We entertained each other . In my work , I painted ‘happy 

scenes’, creating a s torybook world where everything was joyful, pretty and happy. I 

needed the world to be only beautiful; I was making it beautiful. My painting was an 

escape into another world. And plus, these ‘happy paintings’ were acceptable and would 

sell. ”

Despite dif ficult domestic circumstances, Joy’s productivity over the next thirty years 

was remarkable, in both an artistic and business sense. From the very beginning, Joy 

Laking practiced her art with immense self -discipline. Rising about 4:45 a.m. every day 

for ye ars, Joy’s routine was to stuff clothes in the washing machine and settle herself near 

the window in her studio by 5:00 a.m. What followed were four ‘blissful’ hours of 

uninterrupted work. At 9:00 a.m., she returned to the children and the business of sell ing, 

framing, wrapping and shipping her art. 

While the children were preschoolers, she painted again during their ‘quiet time’ between 

1:00 p.m. and 3:00 p.m.. How did she manage to impose this discipline on three 

rambunctious children? “ It was a matter of strict routine and the children accepted it .” 

With this unceasing labour, Joy was able to support her family with her art. Painting was, 

and is, Joy Laking’s passion, but she accepted the trade -off required to make a living. In 

the early 1980’s Joy w as asked to illustrate children’s books. She did two: “ The Brook 

and the Woodcutter ”, an early environmental warning, and “ The Man Who Couldn’t Stop 

Sneezing ”. While she enjoyed illustrating, it didn’t bring in enough money so she looked 

for other avenues to pay the bills, including a very popular series of calendars with 12 of 

her paintings from the year, and limited edition prints. 

During her first years as a fulltime artist, Joy made exquisite flower paintings. Ranging 

from apple blossoms to ladies slip pers to snowdrops, the paintings are as closely detailed 

as botanical illustrations and reveal a delicacy of line and colour, and remarkable 

technical virtuosity, particularly in handling white and pale pinks on white paper. In the 

mid -1980s, she created a series of winter works including white clapboard houses and 

white laundry blowing against white snow. Joy Laking’s unique white -on -white 

technique remains an outstanding achievement. 

Her winter paintings reveal a preoccupation with reflection and an ong oing dialogue 

between light and shade. Absorbed in the qualities of reflected light, and how to capture 

it in watercolour, Joy made many paintings of views seen through windows. Often glass 

bottles on the windowsill are included to add more dimensions to t he light bouncing back 

to the eye. One of Joy’s ‘window’ paintings, “Brigitte’s Window” was chosen as the 

cover for the 1985 Maritime Tel and Tel Directory. 

Since Joy was self -taught in watercolours, she felt free to experiment to achieve the 

effects she wanted. Over time she developed a process of applying paint to get depth, 

tonal contrast and intense colour. “ People think that watercolours have to be washed -out 

pastels. But they don’t. Every layer of paint that the light has to go through before it hit s5

the white paper muddies the colour. I discovered that if you put the darks in first in a 

single layer you will achieve maximum luminosity. Oftentimes, the light takes care of 

itself; a lot of it is white paper.” 

In the late 1980s she and her husband bui lt a gallery on to the house to display her 

paintings. Though the house was out of the way, Joy had become known in Nova Scotia 

by then and both locals and tourists found their way to the gallery. 

In 1990, Joy Laking was invited to do a solo exhibition a t the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia. 

The exhibition then toured for a year. This recognition by a provincial gallery was a 

remarkable tribute to an emerging artist. The honour gave her the confidence to stop 

accepting commissions and paint her own images. By then, she had internalized the 

Nova Scotia scenery and come to love it. Painting on location in the warmer months, she 

captured shoreline and seascape and was also drawn to houses, especially front doors 

with porches and inviting chairs. These paintings a re saturated with domestic pleasure. In 

fact, flower -decked porches became signature pieces for the artist and were immensely 

successful. During this time she also spent a couple of months each year developing an 

image into a serigraph; a handmade silkscre en print. 

Joy sold from her own gallery, and in private art galleries (she was represented by 

Manuge Gallery and Zwickers Gallery in Halifax and Beckett Gallery in Hamilton 

Ontario). In the ten years between 1982 and 1992 she held nine solo exhibitions an d six 

group exhibitions. 

Starting from the mid -1990s, she continued with group exhibitions and shows in her own 

gallery, and began to maintain a website and take online orders. Most years, she made at 

least seventy paintings. Each exhibition meant hours o f work and each sale meant 

framing, packaging, accounting and all the other time -consuming tasks apart from 

painting itself. 

“It is a horrible thing to have to stay alive with your art – to do your art and also pay the 

mortgage. I would just get started on something interesting and have to go back to tend 

to the gallery. In an ideal world, I wouldn’t care if any of my paintings were sold; I just 

like to do the work. Do the work and have them stack up. Maybe I would like to have an 

exhibit after a while, b ut only to see what they look like all together.” 

For Joy Laking, the process of making a painting is the true pleasure; the activity itself 

completely absorbing. “ Painting is a physical activity, but it is also a highly cerebral 

process. You are thinking and solving puzzles all the way along, but in a non -verbal way .

Even before you begin, you have to have your composition – your plan – and you need to 

know where your tonal values are. You are utterly immersed in a world of composition 

and light and tone. If I’m painting indoors, the telephone can ring and I won’t even hear 

it. If I’m painting outside, and people are around and ask me questions, it takes a big 

effort to break my concentration and answer .” 6

Joy Laking maintains a steady rhythm in her painti ng year. If the temperature is above 

freezing, she is usually outside, battered hat on head, searching for an image that catches 

her attention. When it does, she will unpack materials from her backpack, perch on her 

stool and start to work, often remaining in the same spot for the next six hours. These 

works ‘en plein air’ have a particularly engaging spontaneity and lightness. 

In the winter Joy Laking works primarily in the studio using sketches or photos of the 

same scene from different angles. She will play with these images, rearranging them and 

looking to see if a composition for a painting might emerge. This process might take 

days, weeks or, if the emerging image is especially compelling, months. She does not 

usually know why the odd image strikes he r so profoundly. In these cases, she might 

remain with the image through a process extending from a sketch composed from several 

photos, to a 5” x 7” watercolour , to a larger watercolour or (less often) acrylic, to a 

watercolour as large as 3’ x 4’. Ofte n the image gets more generalized, less realistic, as it 

gets bigger. 

In 2006, in a new marriage and having surmounted a serious health issue, Joy is 

experiencing what she describes as an ‘explosion of creativity’ ranging from painting and 

photography to rughooking, wool dyeing, acrylics, oil painting and even beach glass 

work. In fact, the artist’s latest exhibition, “ Here and Away – Seeing with Passionate 

Eyes ” in Truro, Nova Scotia is a photography exhibition, mounted jointly with a fellow 

traveler, and photographer, Laurie Gunn. Joy proposed this dual exhibition to 

demonstrate how photographs taken in the same place at the same time by different artists 

reflect the unique spirit of each. 

Confident in her ability to select compelling images, Joy’s pho tographs are exuberant 

and, like her paintings, rich in colour. Unlike her paintings, though, some of her best 

photographs feature people. She captures the essence of a person, often in movement, in 

his or her setting. Even in close -up, her subjects seem o blivious to the photographer, 

revealing their unique selves. 

Despite her interest in everything creative, Joy remains dedicated to developing further as 

a painter and believes that her work is more serious than ever before. Recent travel has 

enriched her artistically, introducing her especially to new facets of light and colour. 

“Before I painted in Italy, I tended to avoid yellows. After three weeks of painting there, I 

returned home so enamored of yellow tones that I painted my dining room in burnt 

sien a.” 

In her most recent paintings, form and colour dominate the identity of the object painted. 

The colours are getting stronger, the subjects simplified, and the composition more 

abstract or sometimes hyper -realistic. For the viewer, these paintings, with their rich, 

robust colours, are a visual feast. 

To progress as an artist takes courage and determination, particularly when the path leads 

away from an established and popular style. Every new work is a plunge into the 

unknown and may fail. “ It seems t o be part of the creative process that in every piece 7

there is a stage – usually about two -thirds of the way through the painting – where I feel 

it isn’t going to work. I think ‘I’m just making wallpaper’. ‘It’s mediocre and I should 

give up’ It happens ev ery time. But I am pig -headed enough to push on and usually it all 

comes together and I can finish. 

Joy Laking exemplifies the independence of mind and stamina required to succeed as an 

artist, whatever the buying public thinks. “As an artist you have to believe in yourself. 

You have to not care what people say because no matter what they say it may not be the 

right thing. You have to have courage to go against the tide. The only thing that matters 

is how I feel about a painting. I only get a few that rea lly work in my opinion. I produce 

some mediocre ones that most people think are wonderful . The worst of it is that of the 

four best paintings I have done in the last couple of years - in fact that I have ever done -

three remain unsold .” 

As usual, we, t he viewers, lag behind the artist who sees what we do not. The future for 

Joy Laking is unlikely to be repetitions of the past. Working in the too -often neglected 

medium of watercolour, she strives to give shape and colour to the world she sees. With 

her a chievements to date and her determination to go further, we can expect more 

‘trophies’ from this gifted Canadian artist.

“Parrsboro Starry Night”
------------------------

### 2017

**Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking**

![Image 4: “Parrsboro Starry Night” by Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking,   Oil on canvas, 61 cm x 91 cm Limited editioned prints available for sale.](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5fb5571e24edaf5d8fe80cc1/1609968214071-LEOV8IQ0KRXS0HLNZVTR/Joy-Laking-painting-1024x818.jpg)

“Parrsboro Starry Night” by Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking, 

Oil on canvas, 61 cm x 91 cm

Limited editioned prints available for sale.

[Purchase a Print](https://www.parrsborocreative.com/shop/p/cab-parrsboro-starry-night-print)

#### Artist Statement

As a painter, I focus on strong compositions that utilizes the full range of tonal value. During my many years of full-time painting, coupled with my en plein air practice, I have honed my ability to capture the beauty of Nova Scotia and the world. While I paint in watercolour, oil and acrylic, I delight in all things creative.

[Visit the Artist's Website](http://www.joylakinggallery.com/)

![Image 5: Joy-PhotoJuly-2016-1024x1024.jpg](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/5fb5571e24edaf5d8fe80cc1/1609451294113-3J8COEGS1NIXCQS647YO/Joy-PhotoJuly-2016-1024x1024.jpg)

#### About the Artist

Joy Snihur Wyatt Laking was born in Owen Sound, Ontario in 1950. The daughter of an artist, she graduated from the University of Guelph with a major in Fine Art in 1972. Since that time, she has lived and painted professionally in Nova Scotia. She currently resides in Portapique, Nova Scotia where she paints from her home and studio.

Laking has exhibited provincially, nationally and internationally including a solo exhibition at the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia, which was subsequently toured for year. She is an elected member of the Society of Canadian Artists, a founding member of PLANS (Professional Living Artists of Nova Scotia) and she has served two terms on the Board of Governors for the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia.

In 2009, Joy received the Halifax Progress Club Woman of Excellence Award and in 2012, she received the Queens Diamond Jubilee Metal. She is the 2016 recipient of the Port Bickerton artist residency.
